I feel like most subtle details are getting lost in the AI era. We build things without considering their purpose, the nuance, or why we're doing them that way in the first place. While working on this sidebar (all crafted by hand, no AI), I adjusted the padding four times just to make sure everything was completely consistent. 

As designers, our eye for detail and the rationale behind every visual decision remain our biggest advantage over AI-generated designs.

And of course, sometimes the best move is simply to use a pre-made library (building MVP for examle)... but the question always is same “How do we make users feel better here than in other apps? What makes us truly stand out?”

feel we reached an absolute peak with @shadcn of what well designed library do - and for 90% of products on the market is a great fit. But if you want to belong to that top 10%, you need an obsession with detail that no component library can hand you out of the box. You need multiple iterations with someone who has pre-AI design experience and genuinely understands what creates that difference. 

This work can be done only at @figma no doubts about that. We designed process to automated doing a lot of wireframes and prototyping, but we didn't allow coding agents to create UI. 

20/60/20 for the win.

bookmarks.text:
the Head of Design at X just open-sourced his taste (a skill that makes your agent's UI look production-grade)

I broke down how it works ↓

Benji wrote down the hundred small decisions he makes when he designs product UI by hand, so an agent can make them too

the skill is built around one sentence:

"it reads as a real product, simplified to what the viewer needs, framed with intent, and every motion has a cause"

it names the 5 ways agent-made UI goes wrong:
> too much, real words in every cell, packed tight
> too little, a wireframe that doesn't read as a product
> boxed, the whole app shrunk into a card like a screenshot
> flat, everything has the same weight
> bland, your brand's style never shows up

then the agent works in 7 steps, and most of them happen before it writes any code:
1. medium: still or animation, where it sits, what size
2. look: light, dark, blueprint or glass, one accent
3. story: 3 to 5 beats
4. examples: start from the closest of dozens of gold examples
5. screen: a few real words, placeholder lines for the rest
6. choreograph: overlapping beats and a loop that ends where it began
7. rehearse: film it, read every frame, fix what it finds

the agent films its own work, a script creates every frame on a sheet and monitors one-frame jumps and text that doesn't fit its box, which a screenshot can't show

it reads your design tokens too, so the UI uses your real colours, fonts and corner radiuses

he built it by giving the same short prompt to 2 new agents with no other context, one with the skill and one without, then comparing the results side by side

when something looked off, he wrote down what was wrong, updated the skill and ran the whole test again, instead of fixing it by hand

works in Grok Build, Claude Code, Codex and Gemini:
npx skills add benjitaylor/skills --skill stageshow

Benji says most results still take him a few rounds of feedback, and the first pass is already a big step up from what an agent makes on its own

The Binance $5.6B drain is a masterclass in modern EVM exploitation.

It wasn't a complex logic bug. It was an EIP-7702 delegation hijack:

1. Setup: Attacker funds 0x7c86 via Tornado Cash, deploys a sweep contract (0x63e8), and runs three live dry-runs on external wallets.
2. Execution: Attacker submits an EIP-7702 batch with 50 pre-signed authorizations (nonce n to n+49) to hit Binance 14's moving nonce window.
3. One authorization hits. Instantly, Binance 14 (an EOA) is reprogrammed to run the attacker's contract bytecode.
4. Execution looks totally organic: Binance 14 sweeps itself clean. Internal threshold alerts don't trigger because, from the nodes' perspective, the hot wallet is just executing its own transaction.
5. Binance 16 immediately auto-refills 28,000 ETH due to automated treasury rebalance scripts, feeding the exploit loop.

The cold truth: you cannot forge an EIP-7702 delegation list.
For this to execute, the attacker already held the raw private key or unconstrained signing access to Binance 14's HSM/KMS.

But hey, 5.64 billion drained across ETH, BTC, and Tron. 2.54 billion frozen by Tether, Circle, Ripple, and World Liberty within hours.

Code is law until the stablecoin admin keys log in.

Binance got bailed out by the very centralized choke points the cypherpunks warned you about.

Hardware wallets leak your home address.
Centralized exchanges leak the keys to the kingdom.

Self-custody on native, non-delegated chains remains the only honest baseline.

At least you know what to avoid.

Reading the reconstructed bytecode of the Binance EIP-7702 sweeper (`0x63e8...6fae`) is wild.

This wasn't a generic drainer. It was custom-engineered for Binance 14's architecture:

- Leaves exactly 1 ether behind (`bal - 1 ether`) when sweeping ETH so Binance's automated hot wallet queue wouldn't error on gas and trip alarms.
- Uses raw `staticcall` + `continue` loops with custom error codes (`SweepItemFailed`) so one bricked or blacklisted ERC-20 wouldn't revert the $6B batch.
- Includes a custom `callExecute` function to impersonate Binance 14 as controller of an external vault holding $823M in USDC.

They leave a comment: "robberies could be prevented if getaway cars were slower."

You can't fully blame EIP-7702, but it sped up the attack. Without 7702, draining 64 tokens plus an external $823M vault from a live exchange hot wallet meant fighting moving nonces across 70+ transactions. Defense systems would've killed it after tx #3.

With 7702, Lazarus sprayed 50 consecutive nonces in one type-4 payload, turned an EOA into a custom proxy, and atomically swept billions in a single block.

Ethereum core devs built the ultimate getaway car. Surgical state-sponsored engineering.

This could be etched onchain:
`if (bal > 1 ether) { http://to.call{value: bal - 1 ether}(""); }`

bookmarks.text:
Compaction is a mistake.

When an agent's context fills up, tools like Codex and Claude Code compact it:
1. The model prefills the entire session again
2. It writes a summary of everything so far
3. A new session starts from that summary

I measured this on a real ~400k-token session with Opus 5.5:
→ 38 s and $1.99 when the prompt cache has expired
→ 29 s and $0.17 when it hasn't

And the summary is lossy. The exact error message, the file path, the one number you needed is often gone.

So I do something new for Mainplane

Context retrieval works the other way around. Mainplane keeps the full record of every session as a file. When the context fills up, a new session starts right away with one instruction: "You are continuing session X. Retrieve key context from it as you go."

The agent searches the old session and copies the exact lines it needs, when it needs them.

Same session, same model: 15 s and $0.10 to get back to work. It does not depend on a cache hit, and nothing is paraphrased.

This is the bitter lesson applied to agent memory. Don't hand-design what the model should remember. Give it the full record and good tools, and let it decide.

Mainplane is open source (MIT). Link in the first comment.

your codebase is becoming organic architecture. agent contributions grow around the constraints and guardrails you’ve designed. good software engineering matters even more now! and no, the continuous stream of code is not something you have to watch helplessly. be more ambitious and design systems, frameworks, and languages to control the chaos.

Since I'm now blocked by bluey from replying to this thread, I answer here by quote tweet

the openAI construction has more to do with convex integration than anything else.

In convex integration, the oscillations are typically built by hand and the iteration procedure creates wild weak solutions. The non-uniqueness construction of Albritton–Brué–Colombo used an unstable vortex to split solutions apart. The Córdoba–Martínez-Zoroa singularities amplify vorticity across scales by strain. In the openAI paper, a fluid instability is clever made so that the flow itself generates the oscillations: they grow by drawing energy from the background shear. The Reynolds stress then becomes the force that creates the collapsing smooth vortex. Using a physical instability to create the stress in this way has no precedent, and it is what produces a smooth force rather than a merely rough one.

Some on these ideas are in the literature (e.g. Leibovich-Stewartson 1983) but the way they are combined is definitely insane and definitely nowhere in the literature previously.

I also don't know of anyone suggesting that convex integration would play a role in the creation of a blow-up solution like this.

On a technical level, the paper is unbelievable, maybe beyond what a human could have come up with but not beyond human understanding: there are several different groups of pde experts working on understanding it who say that they more or less understand now. I expect digestions soon

td;lr: anyone saying that this OAI result is unsurprising is bullshitting

bookmarks.text:
Working in HTML artifacts has become such a powerful way to do "zoom in" / "zoom out" design work. 

In my experience, design tools have subtly siloed distinct but interdependent design tasks. Because the tools are designed to give you the "best experience" for tackling each kind of problem, you often have to explore different design levers individually.

Instead of isolating design tasks like visual systems, layout choices and interaction design, HTML artifacts allow you to create custom levers to match whatever mental model you're currently using to solve a problem. And when you're done, you can just throw it away.

Today, I'm working on a new theme but also cleaning up some janky looking "just get the functionality in" screens. It's been so helpful to be able to jump between new vs. old theme and new vs. old design to verify the work along the way.

用 HTML 盖栋房子，点一下就展开

到位时那一下轻轻的回落，会让网页里的模型有点重量感。这次参考 Akshat Singh 的404页面，研究它的等距线稿和机械动作手感，主体换成折叠庭院

机械动作要有固定的连接关系

窗框和墙面共用一套转动，整块板一起走，连接处就不会散。屋顶用两块互相铰接的板，后板连在背墙上，折起来也始终接得住

几组动作错开起步，前一组还没停，后一组就跟上，能看出整套机构被带动的过程

一次展开约三秒，末尾保留很小的过冲再落稳。展开后会一直停住，留多少时间看内部，由观众自己决定。收起沿同一条时间线倒着走

制作时还修过一个背景跟着晃的问题，原因是每一帧都按模型当前的轮廓重新居中，部件一展开，整个画面就被带着挪

这里改成按完整动作预留范围，取景的位置和缩放全程固定，底座和网格也就稳住了。零件有了固定的参照，转动的方向和幅度才能看清楚

这类交互适合用在空间概念展示和产品结构演示里，也可以做成网页中的互动插画，让观众自己动手查看一个对象的内部关系
